Here are verse-by-verse notes on 2 Chronicles 10, drawn from the sources retrieved.

---

## 2 Chronicles 10 – Verse-by-Verse Commentary

### Overview

This chapter narrates the division of the united kingdom under Rehoboam, Solomon's son. It corresponds almost word-for-word with 1 Kings 12:1–19. The Chronicler uses this event as the great turning point that opens the story of the southern kingdom of Judah (chapters 10–36).

---

### v. 1 — "Then Rehoboam went to Shechem, for all Israel had gone there to make him king."

- Rehoboam was Solomon's only son mentioned by name (1 Chr 3:10), despite Solomon having 1,000 wives and concubines — a sobering demonstration that sin is a poor way of building a family. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-10/)
- Shechem was chosen because it was the geographical centre of the northern tribes. Meeting there rather than demanding that representatives come to Jerusalem showed Rehoboam was in a position of political weakness. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-10/)
- Shechem carried rich covenantal history: Abraham worshipped there (Gen 12:6), Jacob built an altar and bought land (Gen 33:18–20), Joseph was buried there (Josh 24:32), and Joshua renewed the covenant there (Josh 24). Choosing Shechem honoured the Ephraimites and was a judicious step to remove disaffection. (https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-chronicles-10-commentary) (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/phc/2-chronicles-10.html)
- Iain Duguid notes that Shechem being associated with Jacob/Israel rather than Davidic Jerusalem was already a hint of tensions: "Identity as 'Israel' was deeper than allegiance to a Davidic king in Jerusalem." (https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-chronicles-10-commentary)
- Warren Wiersbe observes that Rehoboam represented the third generation of the Davidic dynasty, "and so often it's the third generation that starts to tear down what the previous generations have built up." (https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-chronicles-10-commentary)

---

### v. 2 — "When Jeroboam son of Nebat heard about this, he returned from Egypt, where he had fled from King Solomon."

- Jeroboam was an Ephraimite whom Solomon had promoted to oversee the forced labour of the house of Joseph (1 Kings 11:28). After the prophet Ahijah told him he would rule ten tribes, Solomon sought to kill him, and Jeroboam fled to Egypt under Pharaoh Shishak's protection. (https://bible.org/seriespage/21-great-divorce-kingdom-divided-1-kings-12-2-chronicles-10)
- The Chronicler omits the background from 1 Kings 11 about Jeroboam's prophetic designation, assuming the reader knows it. (https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-chronicles-10-commentary)

---

### vv. 3–4 — "So they sent for Jeroboam, and he and all Israel came to Rehoboam and said, 'Your father put a heavy yoke on us. But now you should lighten the burden…'"

- The people's complaint concerned heavy taxation and forced labour under Solomon. His vast building projects, extravagant court, and multilayered bureaucracy drained the populace. The request was reasonable, couched in a spirit of fairness and loyalty. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-10/) (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/phc/2-chronicles-10.html)
- Andrew Hill notes that a combination of factors made taxation the flashpoint: loss of revenue from satellite states during Solomon's decline, the cost of Solomon's administration, and royal extravagance. (https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-chronicles-10-commentary)
- David Guzik points out that the elders of Israel made no spiritual demand on Rehoboam — "Seemingly, the gross idolatry and apostasy of Solomon didn't bother them at all." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-10/)
- God had warned Israel through Samuel about what a king would take from them (1 Sam 8:10–19); now they were living under a "taking king." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-10/)

---

### v. 5 — "Rehoboam answered, 'Come back to me in three days.' So the people departed."

- Rehoboam did not commit to a rash reply, which seemed prudent. However, the Preacher's Homiletical Commentary suggests that since the demands were just, prompt redress would have been better than prudent delay. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/phc/2-chronicles-10.html)

---

### vv. 6–7 — Rehoboam consults the elders; they advise kindness.

- The elders were men who had "stood before Solomon" — experienced counsellors familiar with statecraft. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-10/)
- Their advice: "If you will be kind to these people and please them by speaking kind words to them, they will be your servants forever." The elders knew that Rehoboam was not Solomon and could not expect the same deference. If he showed a servant's heart, the people would love him forever. This was sound advice. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-10/)
- The 1 Kings parallel adds the nuance "If you will be a servant to this people today…" — the path to lasting rule was through service. (https://bible.org/seriespage/21-great-divorce-kingdom-divided-1-kings-12-2-chronicles-10)

---

### v. 8 — "But Rehoboam rejected the advice of the elders; instead, he consulted the young men who had grown up with him and served him."

- The text says Rehoboam rejected the elders' advice *before* he ever consulted the young men. This reveals "advice shopping" — asking different people until finding someone who says what you already want to hear. It is an unwise and ungodly way to seek counsel. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-10/)
- Precept Austin notes the "but" here is "one of the more strategic 'buts' in the Bible, for it literally changed the history of the nation of Israel." The Greek OT (LXX) uses *kataleipo* in the active voice — a volitional choice. Here we see the juxtaposition of God's sovereignty and human responsibility. (https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-chronicles-10-commentary)
- The Sermon Bible identifies two things that made Rehoboam's life a failure: (1) he was brought up in the lap of luxury, never knowing hard work or difficulty, and (2) he refused the advice of men older and wiser than himself. "Evil companionship proved his destruction." (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/sermon/2_chronicles/10.htm)

---

### vv. 9–11 — The young men's counsel: harsher oppression.

- The young men who had grown up with Rehoboam urged an adversarial, tyrannical approach. Rather than appealing to shared vision (as Solomon had, despite his burdens), they counselled rule by fear: "My little finger is thicker than my father's waist!" (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-10/)
- A Targum translates this proverb: "My weakness shall be stronger than the might of my father." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-10/)
- "Whereas my father scourged you with whips, I will scourge you with scorpions" — the Preacher's Commentary explains that "whips" were often fitted with sharp bones or lead pieces, while "scorpions" (*scorpio* in Latin) were scourges with sharp iron points that inflicted exquisite pain. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/phc/2-chronicles-10.html)
- G. Campbell Morgan: "He attempted to continue the despotism of his father, though he lacked his father's refinement and ability to fascinate." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-10/)
- Dilday: "With a dozen rash words, Rehoboam, the bungling dictator, opened the door for four hundred years of strife, weakness, and, eventually, the destruction of the entire nation." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-10/)
- Payne suggests the "young men" were "probably some of Solomon's many sons, rendered callous by upbringing in the luxurious harem and court at Jerusalem." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-10/)

---

### vv. 12–14 — Rehoboam answers harshly.

- Rehoboam answered "roughly" — the very opposite of the "kind words" the elders counselled. He forsook the elders' counsel entirely and followed the young men's advice word for word. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-10/)
- Adam Clarke: "Rehoboam was a fool; and through his folly he lost his kingdom. He is not the only example on record: the Stuarts lost the realm of England much in the same way." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-10/)
- John Trapp: "Livy saith, when a state is ripe for ruin, all wholesome counsels are fatally but foolishly slighted." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-10/)

---

### v. 15 — "So the king did not listen to the people, and indeed this turn of events was from God, in order that the LORD might fulfill the word that He had spoken through Ahijah the Shilonite to Jeroboam son of Nebat."

- **The theological crux of the chapter.** The Hebrew word translated "turn of events" (*n'sibbah*) is rare; Ellicott notes it is equivalent to *sibbah* in 1 Kings 12:15, literally meaning "a turn or turning-point (of events) from with God." (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/2_chronicles/10.htm)
- Martin Selman observes this rare word pairs with the verb "turn" in 1 Chronicles 10:14 (the transfer of Saul's kingdom to David). Together these mark two great turning points: the establishment and the fracturing of David's dynasty. (https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-chronicles-10-commentary)
- David Guzik (Enduring Word): "God managed this whole series of events, but He did not make Rehoboam take this unwise and sinful action. God simply left Rehoboam alone and allowed him to make the critical errors his sinful heart wanted to make." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-10/)
- Meyer: "It seemed to be altogether a piece of human folly and passion; but now we are suddenly brought into the presence of God, and told that beneath the plottings and plannings of man He was carrying out His eternal purpose…. He makes the wrath of man to praise Him, and weaves the malignant work of Satan into his plans." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-10/)
- Spurgeon (Baptist/Reformed): "God is in events which are produced by the sin and the stupidity of men. This breaking up of the kingdom of Solomon into two parts was the result of Solomon's sin and Rehoboam's folly; yet God was in it…. God had nothing to do with the sin or the folly, but in some way which we can never explain, in a mysterious way in which we are to believe without hesitation, God was in it all." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-10/)
- Matthew Henry: "This does not at all excuse Rehoboam's folly, nor lessen the guilt of his haughtiness and passion, that God was pleased to serve his own ends by them." (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mhcw/2_chronicles/10.htm)
- The Preacher's Homiletical Commentary adds nuance: neither the king's folly nor the people's rebellion was pre-ordained in a fatalistic sense; men acted as free agents under moral government, not physical compulsion, and remained fully responsible. The "turn of events" from God means events in history are directed to accomplish divine purposes, but human agents remain morally accountable. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/phc/2-chronicles-10.html)
- **Reformed perspective (Ligonier):** The division of the kingdom, though brought about through Rehoboam's foolishness, fulfilled God's word. The lesson for the post-exilic audience of 2 Chronicles was the necessity of serving Judah's king and worshipping at God's appointed place. For Christians, "blessing will come to God's church only insofar as we serve and worship God in and through the Judahite King, Jesus Christ." (https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/rehoboams-reign)

---

### v. 16 — "'What portion do we have in David, and what inheritance in the son of Jesse? To your tents, O Israel! Look now to your own house, O David!' So all the Israelites went home."

- This cry of secession echoes the earlier rebellion of Sheba son of Bichri (2 Samuel 20:1), expressing "deep-rooted aversion to the royal house." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/phc/2-chronicles-10.html)
- Rehoboam's folly caused Israel to reject not just Rehoboam but the entire Davidic dynasty — "Israel's greatest king." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-10/)
- Grant's Commentary notes this separation "has never been repaired and never will until the Lord Jesus returns to Israel at the end of their Great Tribulation." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/lmg/2-chronicles-10.html)
- Matthew Henry draws a spiritual parallel: "Thus is the government of Christ cast off by many, notwithstanding all he has done to bind the children of men for ever to himself; they say, We will not have this man to reign over us." (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mhcw/2_chronicles/10.htm)

---

### v. 17 — "But Rehoboam still reigned over the Israelites living in the cities of Judah."

- This signals the formal division: a northern kingdom of ten tribes (called "Israel") and a southern kingdom of Judah and Benjamin (called "Judah"). From this point forward, the Chronicler's narrative focuses almost exclusively on the southern kingdom. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-10/)
- Matthew Henry notes God's mercy: "When Solomon's iniquity is remembered, and for it his son loses ten tribes, David's piety is not forgotten, nor the promise made to him; but for the sake of that his grandson had two tribes preserved to him." (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mhcw/2_chronicles/10.htm)

---

### v. 18 — "Then King Rehoboam sent out Hadoram, who was in charge of the forced labor, but the Israelites stoned him to death. And King Rehoboam mounted his chariot in haste and escaped to Jerusalem."

- Hadoram (called Adoram in 1 Kings 12:18) was the worst possible envoy — "famous for his harsh policy of forced labor" (1 Kings 4:6; 5:14). "He was probably one of the most hated figures in the land, an embodiment of oppression" (Payne). (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-10/)
- The Speaker's Commentary identifies three distinct persons (Adoram/Adoniram/Hadoram) perhaps from one family, serving under David, Solomon, and Rehoboam respectively. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/phc/2-chronicles-10.html)
- Selman: "Rehoboam makes one pathetic effort to restore unity, perfectly illustrating the poverty of his policy." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-10/)
- Stoning was the "usual mode of mob vengeance" in the ancient Near East. The king himself narrowly escaped the same fate. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/phc/2-chronicles-10.html)

---

### v. 19 — "So to this day Israel has been in rebellion against the house of David."

- "To this day" reflects the vantage point of the Chronicler, writing centuries after the event, for whom the division remained the defining reality of Israel's history. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-10/)
- Two earlier tensions foreshadowed this split: the dispute after Absalom's rebellion (2 Samuel 19:40–43) and the rebellion of Sheba (2 Samuel 20:1–2). (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-10/)
- Knapp: "Rehoboam ought to have been thankful that God's love to David had left him even two tribes." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-10/)
- Gaebelein notes the fulfilment of God's word to Solomon in 1 Kings 11:11–13: "The words spoken to Solomon were now fulfilled." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/gab/2-chronicles-10.html)

---

## Where Protestant Traditions Differ

### Reformed / Sovereign Grace Emphasis (v. 15)

The Reformed tradition (Ligonier, Spurgeon) emphasises that while Rehoboam acted freely and sinfully, God was sovereignly orchestrating events to fulfil His word through Ahijah. Spurgeon's formulation is classic: God was "in" events produced by sin and stupidity without being the author of the sin. Ligonier connects this typologically to Christ: the Davidic dynasty survives only in the Judahite King, Jesus, through whom alone the church finds blessing. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-10/) (https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/rehoboams-reign)

### Wesleyan / Holiness Emphasis

No distinctive Wesleyan commentary on this chapter was retrieved from seedbed.com or wesley.nnu.edu. However, the Preacher's Complete Homiletical Commentary (which broadly reflects 19th-century evangelical homiletical tradition, often used across denominations) stresses that the "turn of events" from God does not imply fatalism: "Men not fated, but free to act; are under moral, not physical government." This preserves the free moral agency that Wesleyan-Arminian theology requires for human accountability. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/phc/2-chronicles-10.html)

### Pentecostal / Charismatic Perspective

EnduringWord.com (David Guzik) serves broadly charismatic and evangelical audiences. Guzik emphasises that God "simply left Rehoboam alone and allowed him to make the critical errors his sinful heart wanted to make" — a reading that fits with both Reformed and charismatic views of divine permission and human free will. No distinctly Pentecostal doctrinal divergence was found from the sources retrieved.

---

## Other Views

### Modern Scholarship

- **Martin Selman** notes that the Chronicler's narrative is not simply repeating Kings but shaping the material to highlight "turning points." The rare Hebrew word *n'sibbah* in v. 15 links with the "turn" in 1 Chronicles 10:14, marking two pivotal transitions in Davidic kingship. (https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-chronicles-10-commentary)
- **Andrew Hill** observes the "literary sophistication" of the narrative: plot (continuation of the monarchy), conflict (threat to unity), character development (Rehoboam's interaction with two sets of advisers), and subplots (Ahijah in 10:15, Shemaiah in 11:1–4). (https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-chronicles-10-commentary)
- **Mark Boda** notes that 2 Chronicles 10 "shatters the idyllic picture the Chronicler has created" in chapters 1–9, introducing a sharp tonal shift that persists through the remainder of the book. (https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-chronicles-10-commentary)

### Catholic and Orthodox Readings

No specific Catholic or Orthodox commentary on 2 Chronicles 10 was retrieved from newadvent.org, catholic.com, or oca.org within the search limits. However, the traditional reading — that Rehoboam's folly split the kingdom but God's providence ruled over all — is shared across all Christian traditions and uncontroversial.
